definition: Inaugurate means to begin something — or install someone in office — with a formal ceremony that marks the start.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word inaugurate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know inaugurate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The city inaugurated its first light-rail line at dawn, with speeches, a brass band, and a ceremonial first ticket.
To open something is the plain, everyday start — weaker than inaugurate, which dresses the same beginning in ritual: an oath, a ribbon, a charter read aloud.
Enthrone goes further than inaugurate: an inaugurated leader takes an oath and an office, while an enthroned one is crowned amid full royal pageantry.

To launch is to send something energetically on its way — a ship, a product, a campaign — with publicity but no required ritual. Inaugurate insists on the ceremony itself: the oath, the ribbon, the charter read aloud.
To commence is simply to begin — the neutral, formal word for events and proceedings, asking nothing of the occasion. Inaugurate wraps the same beginning in ritual and marks it as historic.

To induct is to admit a person into membership — a society, a hall of fame, an order of peers. Inaugurate installs a person in an office or opens something new to the world; you are inducted among equals, inaugurated into a presidency.

The university inaugurated its new chancellor in the stone chapel — robes, the mace carried in, the 1854 charter read aloud — before she signed the register that every chancellor before her had signed.
Inaugurate is never a plain start: it is a beginning dressed in ceremony, whether a person is being installed in office or a building, service, or era is being formally opened.

And watch the prefix — this in- is not the unit's 'not.' It is Latin in-, 'in, on': in Rome nothing official began until an augur read the omens in the flight of birds, and inaugurare meant to install someone once the signs approved.
Inaugurate is the ceremonial word for a beginning — presidents, chancellors, buildings, eras.
If no ritual is in sight, plain open, begin, or launch is more honest; commence is the neutral formal 'begin'; induct admits a person to membership rather than office.

For sixty years, students at Harwood College checked out books from a converted gymnasium.
So when the new library was finally finished, President Ozawa refused to just unlock the doors.
She chose to inaugurate the building properly: a procession of faculty in full regalia, a choir on the steps, and the first borrower's card stamped in front of six hundred guests.
A trustee had argued for skipping the fuss and simply opening on a quiet Monday.
Ozawa overruled him: beginnings this large, she said, deserve to be marked.
Fifty years from now, she told the crowd, nobody will remember a Monday.
Everyone remembers a ceremony.
